description: Fixed curriculum for pnpm eval:agents, so evals don't depend on a fresh Curriculum Architect run. Concept titles match the 'concept' field in lessons/*.json. citeHeading is resolved to chunk ids at load time (chunks whose heading path ends with it). Each concept has one exam question with its reference facts.

modules.title: Blocks and Merkle Trees
modules.goal: Explain what a block header holds and how a Merkle tree commits to and proves a block's transactions.

concepts.title: Block Header
concepts.summary: A block is a small 80-byte header plus its transactions. The header links to the previous block and commits to the transactions.
keyFacts: A block is a container with a small header followed by the list of transactions.
The block header is 80 bytes; the transactions are much larger.
The header contains the version, the previous block header's hash, the Merkle root, a timestamp, the difficulty target and a nonce.
Each header contains the hash of the previous block's header, which links blocks into a chain.
A block is identified by hashing its header twice with SHA256; that block hash is not stored inside the block.
misconceptions: The block header contains a copy of all the transactions.
Blocks are linked by repeating the previous block's transactions.
The block hash is stored as a field in the block header.

exam.question: What does a block header contain, and how does it link a block to the one before it?

concepts.title: Merkle Trees
concepts.summary: A Merkle tree hashes transactions in pairs, level by level, into one Merkle root that is stored in the block header.
keyFacts: The Merkle root is a single hash that summarises every transaction in the block.
Each transaction is hashed; neighbouring hashes are paired, concatenated and hashed again.
Pairing and hashing repeat level by level until one hash, the Merkle root, remains.
Bitcoin's Merkle trees use double SHA256 (SHA256 applied twice).
If a level has an odd number of hashes, the last hash is duplicated.
The Merkle root is stored in the block header; changing any transaction changes the root.
misconceptions: The Merkle root is stored in every transaction.
Changing a transaction doesn't change the Merkle root.
The odd hash out is discarded.

exam.question: How is a block's Merkle root built from its transactions, where is it stored, and what happens to it if one transaction changes?

concepts.title: Merkle Trees and Lightweight Clients
concepts.summary: Lightweight clients keep headers and verify a transaction's inclusion with a short Merkle path checked against the header's Merkle root.
keyFacts: Lightweight clients, such as phone wallets, don't download every transaction; they mostly keep block headers.
To prove a transaction is in a block, a full node sends a Merkle path: the sibling hashes from that transaction up to the root.
A Merkle path needs about log2(N) hashes for N transactions, so it stays small as blocks grow.
The client hashes up the path and checks the result matches the Merkle root in the header it already has.
misconceptions: A lightweight client must download every transaction to verify one.
Merkle proof size grows linearly with the number of transactions.
To prove inclusion you have to send the whole block.

exam.question: How can a lightweight client check that a transaction is in a block without downloading every transaction, and how big is the proof?
